title: Galatia
capsule: Galatia was the region of central Anatolia settled by Celtic Gauls (Galatai) who crossed the Hellespont around 279 BCE under leaders including Leonnorius and Lutarius, and after decades of raiding were confined to a territory around Ancyra, Pessinus, and Tavium by the Seleucid king Antiochus I around 270 BCE. The three Galatian tribes — Trocmi, Tolistobogii, and Tectosages — maintained their distinct tribal structure and Celtic language for centuries while gradually Hellenizing. Rome recognized Galatia as a client kingdom under Deiotarus (d. 40 BCE) and made it a Roman province in 25 BCE after the death of the last king, Amyntas. It became famous in early Christian history as the recipient of Paul's Letter to the Galatians.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territory of the three Galatian tribes is well attested through ancient sources; exact frontiers at any given moment are uncertain because the region was defined ethnically rather than by fixed administrative borders until the Roman provincial organization.
